title: MB0-01424
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, his wife XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and their child XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the claimants) are citizens of the Republic of Haiti. Their son XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is a citizen of the United States.
They are claiming to be "Convention refugees" and "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
XXXXXXXXXXXXXX was appointed as the designated representative of her two minor sons.

The claimants alleged that their house was destroyed and they lost their jobs as a result of the earthquake that struck several parts of their country on January 12, 2010. Despite international aid, there was not enough food, water, medication or shelter for sleeping. People were sent to camps, a number of which had no police or international protection.

The claimants alleged that security in general remains tenuous in the Republic of Haiti, as a number of prisoners escaped from the prisons. Armed gangs have taken control of certain areas and terrorize the region, committing theft, rape, murder and assault. Because of this endemic crime, the claimants lived in fear of being robbed or even killed in their sleep while they were trying to survive.

On XXXXXX, 2010, the female claimant was able to leave Port-au-Prince with her son XXXXX, a US citizen, on a US military airplane. They arrived in the US the same day. The male claimant left Haiti with his son XXXXXXXXXX on XXXXX, 2010, to join his wife in the US. They arrived at the Canadian border together on March 10, 2010, and claimed refugee protection.

Having taken into consideration the Guideline entitled Women Claiming Refugee Status for Gender-Related Reasons,1 the panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection," for the reasons that follow.

In order to establish their identities, the claimants submitted their Haitian and US passports (the originals of which were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada), among other things. The panel has certified copies on file.2 The panel finds that the claimants have provided acceptable documents establishing their identities within the meaning of section 106 of the IRPA.

From the outset, the female claimant stated that she feared the insecurity should she return to her country of citizenship. She stated that her house was destroyed in the earthquake on January 12, 2010; therefore, if she returned to Haiti, she would have to live in a camp, where people are raped and kidnapped, and this would put her life in danger.

The male claimant added a new ground to his claim for refugee protection on the day of the hearing. He stated that he would be a prime target if he returned to his country, because it is recognized that Haitians who return to the country from abroad are perceived as being wealthy. When asked when he had learned this, the male claimant stated that it has always been this way, that it is even a tradition. He stated that people returning from abroad are identified at the airport and then followed and robbed because they are seen as being rich.

In response to question 12 on his Personal Information Form (PIF),3 the male claimant stated that he studied in France in 1995 and 1996. His passport (A-2) indicates that he came to Canada in 2007, and his response to question 12 of his PIF (D-1) states that he stayed in Canada from XXXXX to XXXXXXXX, 2009. He also indicated that he has travelled to the US a number of times in the past 10 years. However, the male claimant testified that he never experienced any problems when he returned to Haiti. How can this be explained, in the context alleged? The male claimant explained that these were short trips that lasted approximately a week and that in 1990 and 1991, the situation had not yet deteriorated; it only became problematic in 2004. When confronted with the fact that he had stayed in Canada in 2009 for at least a month, the male claimant stated that he had experienced no problems when he returned to Haiti.

When asked to explain why he had not included this ground of persecution in his response to question 31 of his PIF (D-1), the male claimant answered that when he had written out his written testimony, he had not been able to think of all the fine details.

As for the female claimant, her passport contains a US visa valid from XXXXXXX, 2007, to XXXXXXX, 2012. She stayed in the US in XXXXX 2007 and from XXXX to XXXXX 2009 and gave XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX kidnapped prior to the earthquake on January 12, 2010. She answered that she had been afraid of this before the earthquake, but that her fear had intensified afterwards. When the question was repeated to her later in the hearing, the female claimant stated categorically that her fear of being raped and kidnapped had started at the time of the earthquake, because they had been particular targets in the camps as the criminals knew that they had travelled in the past and that one of their children was a US citizen. She stated that she slept in a car with her child in order to protect him.

The male claimant was a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The female claimant worked XXXXX as an XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The male claimant was asked whether he could take refuge in another city in Haiti, such as Cap Haïtien or Jérémie, which were not affected by the 2010 earthquake.4 He explained that the organizational structure in Haiti is different from the structure in other countries, as all of the XXXXXXX and government structures are located in Port-au-Prince; there are no organized structures in the provinces. He added that both he and his wife were born in Port-au-Prince and that he had no family anywhere else in the country. The male claimant also stated that because of the earthquake, many Haitians have taken refuge in the provinces, which have become saturated; thus, these locations are all experiencing what has become a national crisis.

Concerning the fear of rape in the Republic of Haiti, although the situation in the country is appalling and was exacerbated by the earthquake on January 12, 2010, the documentary evidence reveals that the situation was no better before the earthquake. The observations made by researcher Cécile Marotte, found at Tab 1.8 of Exhibit A-15 dated November 5, 2008, describe the insecurity that prevails throughout the country. In particular, she states the following: ... The Haitian population lives in a constant state of collective vulnerability that affects them daily. The insecurity is marked by rampant violence that takes various forms, which reduces citizens' collective living space. Families and individuals have withdrawn out of fear or because of threats made against them. ... Currently, the main form of violence in Haiti is kidnapping for ransom, which is sometimes followed by beatings and sexual assault. From 2005 to 2006, many women who were kidnapped were raped. However, ransom is the main objective today. Overt aggression followed by death or disappearances have also been observed. Finally, weapons trafficking, which contributes to organized crime, is another major issue in Haiti.

A 2008 Amnesty International report entitled Don't Turn Your Back on Girls: Sexual Violence Against Girls in Haiti6 tells us that rape has, in the past, been used as a political weapon and that, more recently, gangs have used rape as a weapon to terrorize the population. This report also states that research conducted between February 2004 and December 2005 estimated that 19,000 per 100,000 girls were raped in the greater Port-au-Prince area.

If the female claimant was afraid of being raped and/or kidnapped in Haiti before the January 2010 earthquake, the panel is of the opinion that her behaviour prior to the earthquake is inconsistent with that of a person who fears gender-related persecution.

Indeed, it is well established in the case law that a delay in leaving the country of persecution, a failure to claim refugee protection in a country that is a signatory to the Convention, or a return to the country of persecution significantly undermines the claimant's subjective fear.7 The fact is that the female claimant did not see fit to permanently leave her country of citizenship even though she had travel documents that would have enabled her to do so, despite the already difficult conditions in Haiti before the earthquake. The panel notes the absence of a subjective fear in this respect8 and is of the opinion that this behaviour is not consistent with that of a person who fears gender-related persecution or who fears for his or her life in the country of citizenship.

The claimants stressed the fact that the insecurity, rapes and kidnappings had increased significantly since the January 2010 earthquake, as they were forced to take refuge in a camp when their house was destroyed.

In Josile,9 the Honourable Justice Martineau remarked: ... Had the Board accepted that a risk of rape is grounded in the applicant's membership in a particular social group, then the inquiry should have resulted in a determination of whether there is "more than a mere possibility" that the applicant risks suffering this harm in Haiti.

The panel concurs with the approach taken by Justice Martineau in the above judgment and with that taken by Justice Pinard in Dezameau,10 where he stated at paragraph 29: (29) This is not to say that membership in a particular social group is sufficient to result in a finding of persecution. The evidence provided by the applicant must still satisfy the Board that there is a risk of harm that is sufficiently serious and whose occurrence is "more than a mere possibility".

Tab 1.4 of the National Documentation Package filed as A-1 describes the extent to which Haiti was affected by the earthquake of January 12, 2010. This section of the package describes the particularly difficult conditions in the camps erected following the January 12, 2010, earthquake, mainly in the Port-au-Prince area. Among other things, this document states that the temporary shelters are inadequate and are not safe for women who do not have male protection. Tab 5.8 of Exhibit A-1, entitled Aftershocks. Women Speak Out Against Sexual Violence in Haiti's Camps, also speaks volumes on this subject.

In Dezameau, cited above,11 the Honourable Justice Martineau stated the following: [translation] ... The Board should fully analyze and consider the issue of adequate state protection in the absence of male protection, as may be the case. Naturally, relevant factors must be considered, such as the geographical location (whether outside of Port-au-Prince or in areas not affected by the earthquake) and the applicant's personal situation (whether she will be accompanied by a spouse or living with family) if returned to Haiti.

In this case, the female claimant is accompanied by her husband and would therefore have male protection. The principal claimants both have university educations. Although life in the provinces is not ideal, the documentary evidence12 from reliable, informed sources indicates that, of the total population of eight million, over 600,000 are living in Jérémie, and three-quarters of a million are living in Cap Haïtien. Apart from the insecurity they have cited, nothing in the evidence submitted shows that the female claimant could not settle in Jérémie or in Cap Haïtien and build a new life there with her husband and children. It is certainly not easy to move far away from extended family to settle and take refuge in another part of the country, to find work and to start over again, but it is not unreasonable.

The panel concludes that the female claimant has not demonstrated that she would face a "serious possibility" of gender-related persecution should she return to Jérémie or Cap Haïtien, or that it would be objectively unreasonable to settle there, taking into account her personal circumstances.13

Although the panel feels compassion for the victims of this natural disaster, the female claimant's situation is not comparable to that of a vulnerable woman living alone in a tent in Haiti, who could, because of the particular circumstances in which she finds herself, be persecuted because of her gender.

Both the female claimant and her husband stated that they fear returning to Haiti because of the prevailing insecurity, which has no nexus to any of the Convention grounds. They stated that they are targeted more often than other citizens because they have a higher social status than other citizens in their country.

The evidence reveals that the claimants fear the endemic criminality in the Republic of Haiti. The case law has established that refugee protection claimants returning to their country of citizenship after living abroad do not constitute a particular social group under section 96 of the IRPA,14 nor does this establish that the risk the claimants would face would be any different from that generally faced by the rest of the Haitian population.15

The case law has consistently held that being a victim of crime is not a ground of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA.16 The panel is of the opinion that the fear alleged by the claimants stems from a generalized risk in the Republic of Haiti to which all nationals of that country are subjected indiscriminately. The evidence does not indicate that the claimants faced a different risk than that faced by their fellow citizens. It is well established that a generalized risk of crime that is shared by the entire population of a country does not meet the criteria of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, even though some individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their actual or perceived wealth.17 Therefore, they do not fall under the exception set out in subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii).

The minor claimant's US citizenship was not contested. His designated representative, who is also his mother, did not cite any grounds that could establish that her child, a US citizen, would face a reasonable chance of persecution and/or any risk in the US, a country that is a signatory to the Convention, should he return to his country of citizenship.

Although the panel feels sympathy for this family that lived through the earthquake that struck Haiti on January 12, 2010, it cannot grant the claimants refugee protection on humanitarian and compassionate grounds, as doing so would exceed the panel's jurisdiction.

Having analyzed all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimants did not discharge their burden of establishing that they would face a "serious possibility" of persecution on a Convention ground. They also failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to their lives, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should they return to Haiti.

For all the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimants, XXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" and rejects their claims for refugee protection.

The panel further determines that the child XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, a US citizen, is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" and rejects his claim for refugee protection.
